title: Chris dePloeg in conversation with Jason Hickel about “The Exterminating Empire”
content:
Pakuis de Zwijger

, Monday, November 23rd: :ive with Jason Hickel, 

Ghassan Abu-Sittah

, 

Harriët Bergman

, 

Chihiro Geuzebroek

, 

Max de Ploeg

 and the author!




In collaboration with In collaboration with Pijke ter Laak, join 

Pakuis de Zwijger

 for a conversation with author Chris de Ploeg about his new book, a radical and urgent indictment of the global capitalist system and the imperial violence it unleashes upon people and planet alike. At its core, the book argues that genocide and ecocide are not tragic byproducts of capitalism – they are its fundamental features. 




Together with renowned climate author Jason Hickel (in person), frontline Palestinian surgeon Ghassan Abu-Sittah (joining online) and our moderator, climate justice activist and researcher Harriët Bergman, we will dive deeper into the interconnections of the great challenges of our time–and more importantly, how to fight back. There will also be cultural performances from Chihiro Geuzebroek and brothers Chris and Max de Ploeg, tying their ancestral struggles in Bolivia and Armenia to the global struggle for liberation.

title: In the Public Eye: “Albert Einstein’s ‘Why Socialism?'”
content:
Einstein’s prescient article “Why Socialism?”, first published by Monthly Review in its inaugural 1949 issue, has to say the least, been circulating for some time. Yet it has never been more relevant than today. 

Monthly Review Magazine

 republished the article online in 2009, making the article even more widely available. 

Monthly Review Press

‘ recent reprint, 

‘Albert Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”‘

 stands out, however, for the extremely enlightening and thorough introduction written by magazine editor, John Bellamy Foster. 










Einstein’s perspective links alienation and nuclear annihilation, capitalism to the devastating possibility of omnicide — the destruction of all human life on earth. 

In defiance of those who would like to, not only re-write history, but erase the future, please help us get this book out to as wide an audience as possible.

content:

INTERVIEWS







Coming from Left Field

: “Black Marxism, Class Politics, and the Questions We Cannot Avoid” (Episode 153)













This conversation ranges from the Grenadian Revolution and anti-colonial struggles in Africa to Malcolm X, Black nationalism, identity politics, and the enduring question of whether the left can build an independent political alternative to the Democratic Party. Nimtz also reflects on Lenin’s approach to elections, the meaning of revolutionary parliamentarianism, and why he sees troubling parallels between today’s global conflicts and the period leading up to World War I. This is a wide-ranging, challenging conversation about race, class, imperialism, and the political choices facing the left today….

title: “Cuba, Ever Committed to Just Causes, Deserves the World’s Support”, by Alice Walker and Salim Lamrani, for Znet
content:
By Alice Walker and Salim Lamrani, for 

Znet




Since the triumph of the Revolution in 1959, Cuba has made support for peoples struggling for their emancipation the cornerstone of its foreign policy, consistently assisting nations of the Global South and independence movements worldwide. After breaking the chains of neocolonial domination by overthrowing the dictatorship of Fulgencio Batista, Fidel Castro made internationalism – that is, concrete solidarity with just causes – a national priority. In spite of its modest size and limited resources, and despite the economic siege imposed by Washington beginning in 1960, Cuba has never failed in its duty of solidarity.




Cuba was the first country in the Americas to recognize the People’s Republic of China in 1960, thereby breaking the diplomatic isolation imposed on Beijing by the United States in the Western Hemisphere. That same year, Havana urged the United Nations General Assembly to open its doors to the legitimate representatives of the Chinese people, rejecting the puppet regime of Chiang Kai-shek. Ten years later, beginning in 1970, Canada and Chile, along with other countries in the Americas, would follow the path forged by Cuba, officially recognizing the legitimacy of Mao Zedong’s Revolution. title: Amos Cecchi’s “Monopoly, Finance, and the Crisis of Capitalism: Paul Sweezy and his Legacy”
content:
Just released! The 

new, expanded Italian edition (featuring an afterword by Riccardo Bellofiore)

 of Amos Cecchi’s book on the economic thought of Paul M. Sweezy.




About 

Monopoly, Finance, and the Crisis of Capitalism

: 

Paul Sweezy and his Legacy




This is the first-ever biography of the scholar who brought Marxian theory to the English-speaking world. Born in 1910, his upbringing during the Depression deepened his understanding of capitalism, especially its tendency toward stagnation—the inability of capitalist economies to generate sufficient capital investment to make use of abundant resources, much less produce a harmonious social order. During the Second World War Sweezy taught at Harvard, and doubled as an intelligence officer—until it became clear that his political views would prohibit a future in any mainstream arena. Leaving Harvard, in the midst of the Red Scare, Sweezy boldly co-founded 

Monthly Review,

 where he remained until his death in 2004.










Each of Sweezy’s major works is given a careful reading, from his seminal interpretation of Marxian economics, 

The Theory of Capitalist Development

title: Unrelenting respect for Braverman’s “Labor and Monopoly Capital”
content:
“Revisiting Harry Braverman’s 

Labor and Monopoly Capital

“, for 

Jacobin

, by 

Sophina Clark

 and 

Daniel Judt




“…A Depression-era metalworker and committed socialist who in 1974, two years before his untimely death, published what remains one of the most powerful applications of Karl Marx’s theory of capital to American history — isn’t this the archetype of Antonio Gramsci’s organic intellectual, the worker raised to consciousness through study and struggle? To understand how capitalism works requires journeying into “the hidden abode of production,” Marx wrote, the place where human labor power is consumed. 

Labor and Monopoly Capital

 took this idea seriously. Across twenty meticulous chapters, Braverman explored the process by which capitalists siphoned value out of their workers. This extraction splintered the human being. Body was torn from mind; motions became mechanical; knowledge was locked away in business suites. Here was “the degradation of work in the twentieth century,” as Braverman’s subtitle had it. But alongside degradation ran a second process. As workers were automated out of industrial production, capital furrowed its way into other realms of life. title: Recently reissued: The Rainbow Challenge (Excerpt)
content:
From the Preface to the new edition of 

The Rainbow Challenge

:




“Jesse Jackson’s first presidential primary race in 1984 should have been a wakeup call for the Democratic Party. Without a large campaign chest, money for advertising, or seasoned political consultants he amassed 3.5 million votes (winning nearly the entire popular vote in the Deep South states of Mississippi and South Carolina, registering 2 million new voters, and winning 21 percent of the total votes cast). The press, the pundits, the pollsters, and the Democratic Party elites could not believe that the American people would vote for a Black man, let alone a man with such a progressive message, so they characterized him at first as a charlatan, then as a spoiler, and finally as a candidate who spoke only for African Americans. They had accepted the idea that Ronald Reagan’s election in 1980 meant that the New Deal reforms were over, that the growing polarization of the electorate could not be overcome, and that the Great Society had been defeated. Their marginalization of Jackson’s message of economic and social justice and international peace through cooperation, and their failure to imagine that anything else could be different, ceded the playing field to the Republican right. Walter Mondale’s tepid, neoliberal message could not compete with Reagan’s sunny, simplistic optimism; Reagan won by a landslide
